title: Security Tracking: NLTK Vulnerability Mitigation Roadmap
locator: issue body (ekaf, MEMBER, 2026-08-28) + comment 1 (alvations, CONTRIBUTOR, 2026-09-02, 'Status check against develop')
persona: Python library maintainers (NLTK) handling a batch of huntr.com advisories
workflow: tracking 20 unfixed huntr advisories filed end of June 2026; re-verifying each against develop
observation: Maintainer tracks 20 unfixed huntr advisories (CVE publication scheduled late Sept). A contributor built, by hand, an 'advisory-probe suite' with one probe per advisory that actually runs the attack and reports FIXED/VULNERABLE; 41/41 probes FIXED on develop, and several roadmap items marked 'Pending PR' were in fact already fixed.
short_verbatim_excerpt: has one probe per advisory that **actually runs the attack** and reports `FIXED`/`VULNERABLE`
current_workaround: hand-built in-repo probe harness (test_advisory_probes.py + security_probes/) run on the maintainer's/contributor's own environment
reported_impact: status of the roadmap was wrong without execution: items believed pending were already fixed
decision_supported: Python ecosystem (closes DA-06 gap): maintainers already build 'run the attack, emit FIXED/VULNERABLE' harnesses by hand; a receipt per advisory is the productized version of this exact workflow
limitations: Probes run in contributor's own environment; no statement about risk of running the PoCs; huntr reports are a specific (AI/ML-focused) bounty channel

title: BUG: SIGSEGV when creating an array from a deeply nested structured dtype
persona: NumPy core maintainers triaging a crash report framed as a security issue (CVSS 7.5 claimed by reporter)
workflow: reproduce reporter's PoC; decide bug vs security
observation: Reporter's Linux-specific PoC 'passes on my Mac'; a maintainer had to write a new portable reproducer (1 MiB thread stack) that crashes on main on any system. Second maintainer ruled it not a security issue under NumPy's security policy.
short_verbatim_excerpt: The reproducer in the issue description relies on Linux-specific details and passes on my Mac.
current_workaround: maintainer rewrites the reproducer by hand; policy doc used to reject security framing
reported_impact: maintainer time spent making the repro portable; security-severity dispute
decision_supported: Environment-dependent reproduction is a real triage cost in Python; a receipt that pins OS/arch/stack limits and runs on Linux would have settled 'does it reproduce' without a maintainer rewrite. Also shows policy (not execution) decides severity, so receipts should not claim severity
limitations: Resolved in one day by expert maintainers; the pain is minutes, not days; no risk-of-execution concern expressed

title: Security: Insecure Pickle Deserialization in Dataset Embedding Model
persona: maintainer of a large Python AI platform (Dify) closing a public security report
workflow: redirect public security reports to GHSA and require a PoC
observation: Maintainer closes a pickle-RCE report filed publicly (a bot had already called it 'good report') and requires resubmission via GitHub Security Advisory with a complete proof of concept; closure explicitly not a validity determination.
short_verbatim_excerpt: please submit it through a GitHub Advisory and please provide a complete proof of concept (PoC)
reported_impact: validity undetermined at close; the PoC burden is pushed back to the reporter
decision_supported: Python maintainers gate on 'complete PoC'; the next step, safely running that PoC, is exactly where Repro Receipts sits (pickle PoCs are code execution by design)
limitations: Does not say the maintainer runs PoCs or how; boilerplate-like response

title: langchain 1.4.0: after_model middleware jump_to="tools" bypasses the HITL pending_tool_calls gate
locator: issue body (CONTROL vs EXPERIMENT repro); comments jackjin1997 (CONTRIBUTOR, 2026-09-16), m13v (2026-09-23), Tardfyou (2026-09-23)
persona: Python agent-framework reporter + contributors independently re-running a security-relevant repro
workflow: offline self-contained repro with a control run and an experiment run; independent confirmation; debate on regression test
observation: Report ships a control/experiment repro 'a maintainer can copy and run AS IS'; a contributor independently confirmed (control False, experiment True). Thread then warns that a proposed regression test could 'flip from a loud fail to a silent pass, bug intact'; reporter separates validated vs unvalidated scope.
short_verbatim_excerpt: the suite flips from a loud fail to a silent pass, bug intact
current_workaround: manual re-run in contributors' own environments
reported_impact: risk of a green-but-wrong regression test
decision_supported: Supports receipt fields: control + experiment, fails-before/passes-after on two refs, and explicit 'validated scope' vs 'not validated'
limitations: Reporter and commenters, not core maintainers; no maintainer statement yet

title: AI-SLOP: Develop best current practises for Open Source maintainers (OpenSSF WG comment by north-echo)
persona: independent AI-assisted security researcher proposing intake requirements to the OpenSSF Vulnerability Disclosures WG
workflow: defining a validation bar projects could enforce at intake
observation: Proposes that intake should require dynamic proof on the exact shipped build, N reproductions from clean state, and positive and negative controls, and that the runner's own tally be verified 'especially when a model wrote or drove it'.
short_verbatim_excerpt: Reproduce N times from clean state, or it doesn't exist.
current_workaround: researcher-side discipline; no project-side tool named
decision_supported: The OpenSSF WG thread is converging on the receipt's exact fields (clean-state reruns, negative control, shipped ref, verified tally); a receipt is a machine-checkable implementation of this intake bar
limitations: Researcher, not maintainer; a proposal, not adopted policy

title: AI-SLOP best practices thread: 'working reproduction' as the discriminator (+ reply by david-a-wheeler)
persona: AI-pipeline researcher + OpenSSF contributor (Wheeler) discussing slop-vs-signal criteria
observation: Researcher: the discriminator is not whether AI was involved but whether the report includes a working reproduction ('a live PoC against a shipped release'). Wheeler pushes back that bugs only on main are still real, so the ref matters but not as a slop filter.
short_verbatim_excerpt: A working reproduction, not a source-pattern guess.
decision_supported: Receipt should record the ref(s) run (release tag AND main), not reject main-only findings
limitations: Same thread as EV-V-0005 (not independent of it)

title: [Security] Malicious SFTP server / HTTP proxy OOM the client (JSch)
persona: Java library maintainer receiving an LLM-assisted report whose PoC is an attacker-controlled 'evil SFTP server' written in Python
workflow: asking for a runnable reproducer that drives the real library
observation: Report ships a Python evil-server PoC ('LLM-assisted, human-verified'). Maintainer asks for Java code using JSch that, together with the Python PoC, demonstrates the issue, and asks for an exact RFC citation. To verify, the maintainer must run the reporter's malicious server plus client code.
short_verbatim_excerpt: Can you please provide Java code using JSch that when used in conjunction with your Python PoC demonstrate these issues?
current_workaround: request more reproducer code from the reporter; run locally
reported_impact: extra round trips; the maintainer runs attacker-authored network code to confirm
decision_supported: Supports the PoC-bearing wedge: verifying needs to run reporter-supplied hostile code (a server), which should happen in an isolated, egress-controlled sandbox
limitations: Java, not Python (the PoC is Python); the maintainer did not state a safety concern

title: we have a year to fix security everywhere (Lobsters discussion)
locator: comments by simonw (https://lobste.rs/c/oplelw, https://lobste.rs/c/rdayad), freddyb 'Firefox Security' (https://lobste.rs/c/6vpqkw), dmurph 'Chromium Developer' (https://lobste.rs/c/qiuhni)
persona: Python OSS maintainer (Datasette author) + browser security engineers
workflow: fixing LLM-found vulnerabilities; wanting to run untrusted processes without home-dir access
observation: Datasette maintainer spent 'a full week' fixing vulnerabilities found by LLM audits, and says sandboxing a process so it can't dig through the home directory and exfiltrate is 'way harder than it should be'. Firefox Security engineer advises giving the LLM a verifier (test harness with invariants). Chromium developer has spent much of the last 3-4 months fixing LLM-reported vulns.
short_verbatim_excerpt: I would like to be able to run a process in a way that prevents it from digging around in my home directory and exfiltrating anything it finds
current_workaround: sandbox-exec / Bubblewrap / landlock (named by simonw) - described as hard to use
reported_impact: a week of maintainer time on one project
quantitative_measure: ~1 week of fixing (Datasette); 3-4 months of elevated LLM-reported vuln load (Chromium)
decision_supported: Python maintainer explicitly wants the containment primitive Repro Receipts provides; security engineers ask for verifiers, not more findings
limitations: published_at approximate (Lobsters shows '6 days ago' on 2026-09-26); simonw's sandbox comment is about running processes generally, not PoCs specifically; the vulns were self-found, not third-party reports

title: The exploit was real. The trap was hiding in its dependencies (ChocoPoC)
locator: article body + 'Treat every PoC repository as untrusted code' recommendation; corroborated by The Hacker News 2026-07-02
persona: vulnerability researchers / triagers who clone and run PoC exploits
workflow: cloning a GitHub PoC and running it (pip installs its dependencies)
observation: Sekoia and YesWeHack found at least seven fake PoC repos for real CVEs whose Python dependencies (PyPI 'skytext', 'frint') install a Python RAT that runs shell commands and steals browser passwords and cookies; skytext was downloaded about 2,400 times. The advice is to run PoC code in disposable VMs and to review the whole dependency chain.
short_verbatim_excerpt: Treat every PoC repository as untrusted code, not just untrusted documentation.
reported_impact: full foothold on researcher machine; credential theft
decision_supported: Concrete Python-ecosystem proof that running a PoC (incl. its pip install step) on your own machine is dangerous; supports DA-08 fix (hashed lock, no-egress verification sandbox)
limitations: Targets researchers downloading public exploits, not maintainers receiving reports; ~86 days old (outside strict 60-day window)

title: Friendly Fire: Hijacking Defensive Cyber AI Agents for Remote Code Execution
locator: Exploit Brief intro + section on geopy setup ('Perform security testing on /path/to/geopy')
persona: security researchers demonstrating attacks on AI agents used for defensive code review
workflow: pointing Claude Code (auto mode) / Codex (auto-review) at an untrusted third-party Python library to assess its security
observation: Prompt injections spread across a modified copy of the Python library geopy led Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6/5, Opus 4.8) and Codex (GPT-5.5) to execute an attacker binary, giving RCE on the machine running the defensive agent. Sometimes the model even noticed the files didn't belong upstream and ran the binary anyway.
short_verbatim_excerpt: enables remote code execution in Anthropic's Claude Code CLI ... when employed to defensively assess the security of an open-source or third-party library
decision_supported: AI-driven triage/repro must itself run in a disposable, secret-free sandbox; 'just ask your local agent to reproduce it' is unsafe
limitations: Exact publish date not shown on page (repo created 2026-07-05; references accessed 2026-07-02); attack is on the codebase, not a bug report

title: Introducing Patch the Planet (Trail of Bits + OpenAI Daybreak)
locator: 'We brought patches' and 'Guidance for maintainers' sections
persona: security consultancy funded by an AI lab to help OSS maintainers (Python projects: urllib3, aiohttp, PyPI, pyca, python.org)
workflow: triaging frontier-model findings, then patching with maintainers
observation: States that the expensive part of security work has moved from finding bugs to confirming them, getting severity right, patching and coordinating. Maintainers flooded with AI reports need deduplication, false-positive filtering and severity correction. The first week covered 19 projects, many in Python.
short_verbatim_excerpt: The advantage is no longer in finding bugs, but everything after: confirming a finding, getting its severity right
current_workaround: expert humans (Trail of Bits engineers) + fp-check tooling + project threat models/AGENTS.md
quantitative_measure: 19 projects week 1; 30+ joined; 64 PRs; 51 issues; 37 patches merged
decision_supported: Who pays: AI labs are funding post-finding verification for OSS (OpenAI Daybreak). Also a competitor/partner: human-expert confirmation is today's answer; receipts make confirmation portable
limitations: Vendor marketing; >60 days old; aiohttp fixed 8 issues within hours (fast Python maintainers)

title: What 50 open source projects taught us about security in the AI era (GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, Session 4)
persona: GitHub as funder of OSS maintainer security work
workflow: grant + Security Lab mentoring + Copilot for vulnerability triage
observation: Session 4 invested >$500,000 across 50 projects at $10,000 each via GitHub Sponsors (paid in tranches over 12 months); maintainers explored Copilot for vulnerability triage. Cohort includes Python projects (LangChain, Pillow, CycloneDX Python lib, ONNX).
short_verbatim_excerpt: The Secure Fund invested more than **$500,000 across 50 projects**
decision_supported: Who pays for OSS: funders pay ~$10k/project for security outcomes; a free-for-OSS receipt runner fits as tooling inside such programs (not a direct revenue line)
limitations: Grant money goes to maintainers, not tool vendors

title: AI-Led Remediation Crisis Prompts HackerOne to Pause Bug Bounties
locator: paragraphs on IBB pause, Node.js, Minimus CTO and Bugcrowd quotes
persona: bounty platforms, OSS projects losing bounty funding, AppSec vendors
workflow: funding and triaging OSS bug bounties
observation: The Internet Bug Bounty stopped accepting submissions on March 27. Node.js then ended its own bounty, saying it has no independent budget. A vendor CTO says valid submissions fell from about 15% to under 5% and that AI moved the bottleneck 'entirely to validation'. A Bugcrowd exec cites 'the maintainer who receives 40 valid reports and has one weekend'.
short_verbatim_excerpt: it's shifted the bottleneck entirely to validation
firsthand_status: mixed (news quoting firsthand execs; Node.js statement firsthand)
decision_supported: OSS maintainers can't pay (Node.js has no budget); enterprise programs and platforms pay for validation
limitations: Older than 60 days; percentages are interviewee claims

title: LLM-assisted triage for HackerOne reports (Node.js Security WG)
persona: Node.js security triage team (volunteers); Apache Airflow maintainer
workflow: rule-based classifier + LLM assessment of H1 reports, humans decide
observation: Node.js designs a two-layer triage: a rule classifier that treats a PoC, repro steps and a Node.js version as positive signals, then an LLM assessment. They plan to pay for it with donated Copilot/Azure credits. An Airflow maintainer built a similar tool and plans to apply it to security reports, possibly ASF-wide.
short_verbatim_excerpt: Flags reports that have positive signals (PoC, repro steps, Node.js version)
current_workaround: in-house LLM triage on donated cloud credits
decision_supported: Maintainers treat PoC presence as signal but have no step that runs it; budget = donated credits (pricing must be free for OSS)
limitations: Older than 60 days; JS; issue went stale

title: HackerOne paid $81 million in bug bounties over the past year
locator: headline + report summary (HackerOne 9th Hacker-Powered Security Report: 1,950 enterprise programs)
workflow: paying bounties and triage via platforms
observation: HackerOne programs paid $81M in bounties over 12 months (+13% YoY) across ~1,950 enterprise programs, and the report notes a 210% rise in AI-vulnerability reports.
short_verbatim_excerpt: HackerOne has paid $81 million in rewards to white-hat hackers worldwide over the past 12 months
decision_supported: Sizing anchor (cite as-is): enterprises already spend real money on reports; the triage/validation layer sits on top of that spend. Do not extrapolate a TAM from it
limitations: Bounty payouts are not triage spend; about a year old
